## Tuesday — the case, part 2

The staged decision points continue from Week 14. At each reveal your team commits to a
decision **before** seeing what happened next. The record of what you decided, and when, is
the material for the debrief — a case handed over complete is a reading assignment, not a
diagnosis.

Bring your Week 14 diagnostic worksheet. You will be asked to defend a call you made before
you knew the outcome.

## Thursday — evidence adjudication panel

Three contested claims. For each, both sides come with primary papers, and teams are assigned
a side they did not choose.

| # | The claim | For | Against |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | "99.5% of megaprojects fail" | Flyvbjerg (2021) base rates, 2,062 projects | Chapman (2024, 2025) Scandinavian data; Love, Ika et al. (2019) |
| 2 | "Agile outperforms predictive" | Gemino et al. (2021); Koch et al. (2023) meta-analysis | Badran et al. on cost performance; Serrador & Pinto (2015) qualifications |
| 3 | "Top management support is the dominant success factor" | Young & Jordan (2008); Young & Poon (2013) | Blaskovics et al., LASSO-ranked factors |

: {tbl-colwidths="[5,35,30,30]"}

::: {.callout-note}
## How this is scored
The rubric rewards students who state **what evidence would change their mind**. It does not
reward picking the side that turns out to be better supported. A team that argues its assigned
side well *and* names the finding that would defeat it scores higher than a team that happens
to be right.
:::

## The eight-step diagnostic protocol

The protocol from Week 14, reproduced here because you will use it on the final:

1. Establish what "failing" means to whom — which success dimension is actually missing.
2. Separate the forecast from the performance: was the plan wrong, or the execution?
3. Reconstruct the baseline and check whether one exists at all.
4. Identify the measurement regime — what is being counted, and what is not.
5. Locate the decision points where information was available and not used.
6. Distinguish structural causes from personnel causes; most attributions get this backwards.
7. Rank candidate interventions by expected effect given the evidence base, not by convention.
8. State what you would need to observe to know your diagnosis is wrong.
